subsystems.name: Encoding layer
subsystems.role: converts digital bits into DNA base sequences and adds redundancy.

subsystems.name: Writer
subsystems.role: inserts the encoded DNA into a host genome.

subsystems.name: Host cell
subsystems.role: the living chassis that stores and replicates the data.

subsystems.name: Archive
subsystems.role: keeps cells alive but dormant for long periods.

subsystems.name: Reader
subsystems.role: recovers and sequences the stored DNA.

subsystems.name: Decoder
subsystems.role: reconstructs the original file from sequencing reads.

buildSteps.title: Encode the data
buildSteps.detail: Split the digital file into blocks, add error-correcting code, map each block to a sequence of A, T, G and C, and attach primer sites so any block can be retrieved on its own.

buildSteps.title: Design the writing strategy
buildSteps.detail: Choose safe insertion sites in the host genome, then design guide RNAs and donor DNA templates that direct the CRISPR system to those sites.

buildSteps.title: Prepare host cells
buildSteps.detail: Grow a dormant cell line and make it competent to take up the CRISPR components and donor DNA.

buildSteps.title: Write the data
buildSteps.detail: Introduce the CRISPR machinery and donor DNA. The system inserts data blocks into the genome. Repeated rounds can add more blocks, but each round risks damaging the cell.

buildSteps.title: Select and verify
buildSteps.detail: Use antibiotic or fluorescent markers to find cells that took up the data, then sequence the targeted regions to confirm the insertions are correct.

buildSteps.title: Archive the cells
buildSteps.detail: Freeze or dry the culture and store it under controlled conditions so the cells stay dormant and genetically stable.

buildSteps.title: Retrieve the data
buildSteps.detail: Revive the cells, extract their DNA, amplify the inserted regions with the primer sites, and read them with a DNA sequencer.

buildSteps.title: Decode
buildSteps.detail: Convert the sequencing reads back into bits, correct errors, and reassemble the original file.

prerequisites.why: Needed to make the donor DNA and guide sequences; current synthesis is accurate for short pieces but costly and error-prone for long ones.
The only practical way to write into a living genome, but payload size and the number of simultaneous edits are still limited.
Reading the data back requires fast, cheap sequencing; current platforms are good but not yet at archive scale for living cells.
DNA storage suffers insertions, deletions and substitutions, so robust codes are still being developed for in vivo use.
Cells must stay dormant and genetically stable for decades; cryopreservation works but is energy-intensive and not proven over centuries.

prerequisites.tech: In vivo writing of large datasets
prerequisites.why: No one has written more than a few kilobytes into a living genome with high fidelity, and random access at scale is unproven.

pathway.milestone: In vitro DNA data storage stores small files in synthetic DNA outside cells.
pathway.unlocks: Proof that DNA is an extremely dense and durable medium for digital data.

pathway.milestone: In vivo recording of small data such as images or text into bacterial genomes using CRISPR.
pathway.unlocks: Biological memory that replicates along with the cell, without external synthesis.

pathway.milestone: Scalable, high-fidelity writing of megabytes into living cells with reliable random access.
pathway.unlocks: A practical archival medium for cold data that is rarely read.

pathway.milestone: Petabyte-scale biological archives that last centuries with minimal power.
pathway.unlocks: A replacement for tape and disk in long-term, low-energy storage.
